content:
OpenAI has just detailed how it will comply with the EU's AI Act, which requires providers of generative AI systems to add identifiable markers to AI-generated text. Here's what you need to know.

Some background

A few months ago, Anthropic sparked controversy by saying that to comply with the EU AI Act, Claude would watermark text by making slight adjustments to word choice.

Basically, Claude would occasionally select between several equally fitting words based on a hidden pattern, which Anthropic said has no practical impact on the meaning, quality, or readability of the response.

Anthropic also built a detection tool that can spot the pattern in a block of text, indicating that it was very likely written by Claude.

)

At the height of the controversy, Anthropic emphasised that Claude wasn't going it alone, saying several other major AI providers were also implementing marking systems to comply with EU requirements.

Today, OpenAI revealed its approach, which is similar but much more limited in both scope and applicability.

OpenAI's text watermarking system

According to OpenAI, "Starting today, API customers worldwide can choose to enable text watermarking for specified models," and the company will "be adding invisible watermarking to eligible ChatGPT and Codex text outputs in the EU in the coming weeks."

So on the API side, text watermarking remains opt-in for now, while for ChatGPT and Codex, it will initially only be enabled for eligible users in the EU.

OpenAI has also opened applications for its text watermark detection tool, initially only to approved researchers and professional organisations, so the company can evaluate and improve the technology.

On accuracy, OpenAI is clear that the detection still has obvious limits, such as false negatives and false positives, which are more pronounced with shorter text or content in specific domains, "like mathematics where word choice is more constrained."

Here's how OpenAI describes textGrain (its text watermarking technology):

The company also notes that watermarks are harder to detect in shorter passages, and editing can significantly weaken the watermark's effectiveness:

Interestingly, when OpenAI compared watermarked and non-watermarked text, the watermarked outputs actually scored slightly higher across multiple benchmarks, though the company says it found no significant difference in overall performance.

Benchmark Unwatermarked text (Astra, max) Watermarked text (Astra, max) Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 49.57 points 49.76 points AutomationBench 34.09% 34.86% DeepSWE v1.1 72.80% 71.68% Terminal-Bench 4.0 53.90% 56.06% Terminal-Bench Science 0.1 56.90% 60.00% BrowseComp 87.92% 87.35% HealthBench Professional 64.27% 64.60% GPQA Diamond 94.44% 93.94%

OpenAI also stresses that beyond the drawbacks of false negatives and false positives, watermarks "do not measure the degree of human involvement," "do not establish ownership or responsibility," "do not identify users," and "do not verify accuracy."

OpenAI adds that "the absence of a detected watermark does not mean text was human-written."

Finally, the company says it expects to revisit its approach as technology, standards, and evidence evolve, while continuing to study how watermarks hold up after editing and translation, and whether they can more effectively distinguish AI assistance from AI authorship.
